subject: elephant
pitch: A gentle African elephant calf. Wrinkly slate-grey skin with a dusty, reddish tint from rolling in the dirt, huge fan-shaped ears with a pink flush on the inside, a curious trunk curling forward, stubby baby tusks, long lashes over kind brown eyes, a little tufted tail and round, padded feet with pale toenails.
reasoning:
I'm planning the structure for a stylized African elephant calf built from primitives in three.js—sizing it realistically at roughly 1.1m shoulder height and 1.3m length, oriented facing +Z with the trunk forward and tail back.

I'm working out the body geometry now, deciding on a scaled, low-poly sphere for the torso with approximate dimensions (around 0.3m horizontal radius, 0.27m vertical radius, 0.45m z-depth) centered around y=0.7 to form a rounded, blocky calf body with the belly sitting above the leg height.

Next I'm shaping the head as a large sphere positioned forward and up near the shoulders, blended into the body through a neck bulge, then moving to the legs, which I'm building as tapered cylinders with rounded feet positioned at the four corners under the body.

For feet, I'm flattening spheres into pads touching the ground, adding small pale toenail shapes on the front edge (four on front feet, simplified), and making sure leg cylinders extend up into the body volume so they overlap cleanly rather than leaving gaps.

Now I'm checking leg radii and thickness for that column-like elephant look, then moving to the ears. For the fan-shaped ears, I'm considering using a custom 2D shape extruded thinly, narrow where it attaches to the head and flaring outward into a rounded fan outline.

I'm working out how to render the two-toned ear: a grey outer face and a pink inner panel. Simplest approach is two separate shapes — a slightly larger grey outer piece and a smaller, inset pink piece layered on the inward-facing side so the pink peeks through near the head.

Actually the cleaner solution: two single-sided plates with the same outline, grey one offset slightly outward facing out and pink one offset slightly inward facing in, so each side of the ear naturally shows its correct color while the opposite face gets culled.

For the ear shape itself, I'm setting up a local coordinate system where the attachment edge sits at x=0 along the head, then extending outward into a rounded fan shape using a Shape path.

Now I'm working out how the ear's flat plate should be oriented in world space—since the ear is wide vertically and fore-aft but thin outward, its local width axis needs to map onto the outward direction from the head, which requires some care with the rotation mapping between shape-local axes and world axes.

I'm sizing the fan shape at around 0.28m radius for a believable big elephant-ear look on the calf, then positioning the pair near the top sides of the head and figuring out the tilt rotation to flare them outward convincingly.

Reconsidering the geometry, the ear plate actually sits in the YZ plane with its flat face normal along X, attached near the top of the head and fanning downward and backward, offset outward from the head surface.

Drawing the fan outline with bezier curves...

Checking proportions - the ear comes out around 0.3 by 0.4, reasonable for a calf's head. Now I'm figuring out where to position the ears relative to the head center in world coordinates.

The ear overlaps the body slightly at that position, which seems fine for flapping against the side, but I should tilt it outward so the bottom flares away from the body. I'll shift the ear group to around x=0.22-0.24 with an added rotation so the geometry angles outward from its base.

For the actual implementation, each ear needs its own group with position and rotation set so the mirrored normals point correctly outward for left versus right—right ear rotation needs to flip sign, and I realize the shape itself needs mirroring (not just rotation) to keep the front-facing side correct, which means using a negative scale on one axis and letting the renderer handle the flipped winding order.

Working out the Z-axis tilt math: for the left ear to flare outward, I need positive rotation.z, and the right ear needs the negative of that angle. I also need to account for how three.js composes Euler rotations (Z applied before Y in local space) so the tilt and the sideways orientation don't fight each other.

Actually, nesting groups is clearer: an outer pivot handles the tilt rotation while an inner mesh handles the base orientation rotation, avoiding the Euler order confusion entirely. For the ear geometry, I'm using ShapeGeometry with the bezier curve segments controlling smoothness.

Now I'm working out the plate offsets—with the mesh rotated so the shape's z-axis maps to world x, placing the grey outer plate and pink inner plate requires careful sign handling since the left and right ears are mirror images. I realize using the same geometry with the same offset signs will put the grey plate outward for the left ear but inward for the right ear, so I need to either flip the rotation sign or swap the offsets specifically for the right-side ear to keep grey consistently on the outside.

For material sides, I'll use DoubleSide on both plates since they're thin and separated, so backface normal flipping won't cause lighting issues. I'm also considering scaling the pink plate down slightly (around 0.86) relative to the grey one so a thin grey rim peeks out from underneath, giving a subtle inset edge effect.

For the trunk, I'll skip adding wrinkle details on the ear and instead build a custom tapered tube: rather than relying on TubeGeometry's constant radius, I'll sweep rings manually along a CatmullRomCurve3 path with a radius function that shrinks over the length, computing frames via a reference vector and cross products since the trunk curve stays mostly in one plane, then assembling the ring vertices into a BufferGeometry with computed normals.

I'm plotting out the actual curve points for the trunk — starting thick at the root near the head, curving forward and down, then curling slightly upward and inward at the tip — along with a tapering radius from root to tip.

Writing tube ring geometry...
